Full Rated refers to the selectivity of protection. For example, consider a circuit breaker here with a 100-ampere rating and 65kA breaking capacity. If a short circuit occurs downstream and the short-circuit current at both breakers is around 60kA, both breakers will trip.

In contrast, Series Rated works differently. For instance, the upstream breaker may have a 65kA rating while the downstream one is rated at 22kA. When the downstream short-circuit current is 20kA, only the downstream breaker trips. However, if the short-circuit current reaches 60kA, the downstream breaker’s insufficient breaking capacity will cause the upstream breaker to trip, resulting in poorer protection selectivity.

The advantage of a Series Rated system lies in cost savings. There is a significant price difference between 20kA and 65kA breakers, and higher-capacity breakers also occupy more physical space. Adopting a Full Rated solution to meet selectivity requirements often necessitates a substantial increase in panelboard dimensions.

Circuit breaker trip mechanisms come in various types, and their breaking capacity and physical size directly impact system design and cost. Selecting a solution requires balancing protection selectivity and economic efficiency.

For example, thermal-magnetic tripping and electronic tripping. Generally, electronic tripping is suitable for applications with currents of 400A or higher. Electronic tripping offers better selectivity and can provide multiple protection functions.

Commercial-use motors are typically smaller in power, generally below 100 kilowatts, and thus have relatively relaxed protection requirements.

Full-pole (Full Pro) circuit breakers refer to the four-pole type, used to disconnect the neutral line. However, such circuit breakers are relatively rare and usually appear in automatic transfer switch (ATS) systems.

A crucial parameter of circuit breakers is their interrupting capacity. In North America, the minimum standard for interrupting capacity is 10kA (10,000 amperes), with a maximum reaching 65kA—typically sufficient for low-voltage applications.

Protection types or protection levels can be categorized as follows: instantaneous protection, short-time delay protection, long-time delay protection, ground fault protection, and overload protection. Multi-pole protection is usually configured at the main switch position, characterized by higher capacity and equipped with an electronic tripping unit, while also providing backup protection for downstream loads. This combination of protections is referred to as LSIG, representing long-time delay, short-time delay, instantaneous, and ground fault protection.

Beyond protection functions, circuit breakers also feature auxiliary control characteristics, such as:

1. Shunt Trip: The breaker incorporates a built-in relay (e.g., a G-type relay) that automatically triggers tripping upon receiving a signal. This function is commonly used in high-voltage systems (more complex in low-voltage systems), with typical applications including generator or load shedding. For instance, when the capacity of an emergency generator bus is limited, a signal can trigger the breaker to trip and shed loads during emergencies.

2. Auxiliary Switch: Monitors the open/closed status of the breaker and outputs signals for system monitoring.

3. Under Voltage Release: Provides low-voltage protection, often used in Automatic Transfer Switches (ATS) to monitor switching signals between system voltage and generator voltage.

4. Alarm Switch: Outputs alarm signals under abnormal conditions.

5. Mechanical Interlock: In dual power supply systems (commonly referred to as “Min-Tai-Min”), mechanical interlocks ensure that two switches cannot close simultaneously, maintaining a one-open-one-closed state.

This interlocking can be achieved mechanically or electronically, such as through Kirk-Lock. Typically, circuit breakers are categorized into different types based on their application scenarios. For example, breakers used in switchgear, switchboards, or motor control centers (MCCs) belong to different categories from those used in ordinary distribution panels. Regarding circuit breaker selection, feeders are typically sized at 125% of the load rating, which also applies to dry-type transformers. For non-motor loads, the standard sizing is 125%; whereas for motor loads, 250% is generally required to account for the impact of equipment starting currents.

When circuit breakers are used to protect circuits consisting of Variable Frequency Drives (VFDs) and motors, specifications often lack detailed guidance. Based on experience, there are two scenarios:

1. With a VFD, since starting current issues are resolved, the current is significantly reduced, allowing breaker selection at 125% of the load value.  
2. If the VFD has a bypass function, the system will switch to bypass operation during VFD failure. In this case, sizing at only 125% without VFD involvement may cause the breaker to trip during motor startup.

Thus, specific analysis is required: 125% can be used when there is no bypass function, but with bypass functionality, 250% sizing is recommended.

If the circuit breaker is used for equipment protection, it must be selected based on the Maximum Overcurrent Protection (MOP) value. Equipment manufacturers usually provide relevant data, and breaker selection should follow MOP parameters—for example, when protecting devices like FARPump.

The selection is typically based on 600% of the composite current, primarily to avoid locked-rotor current and starting current. This equipment does not have fire pump functionality. The VFD controller then adjusts the fan speed—increasing it when pressure falls below the setpoint or decreasing it when pressure exceeds the setpoint—to maintain system pressure stability.
